newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia vows further reforms to support growth.
newsitem.headline: Croatia vows further reforms to support growth.

text.p: Croatia's government vowed on Monday to step up economic reforms to ensure the ex-Yugoslav republic's economic recovery would continue after a three-year period of relative stability.
"This is not easy, but there is no alternative," Prime Minister Zlatko Matesa told a news conference marking his first anniversary in office.
"Perhaps inflation can finance economic growth in the short term...but if we allowed it now, in a few years we would have to launch another stabilisation programme," he said.
Annual inflation has been curbed to an average 0.7 percent since 1993 and was down at just 0.1 percent in September on a monthly level.

Industrial output has recovered after a sharp drop caused by the four-year war in the former Yugoslavia that ended last year. Propelled mainly by a strong gain in services such as tourism and transport, the economy also posted some growth.

To ensure the financing of future growth, officially forecast to reach at least seven percent this year, Matesa said the government would press on with the overhaul of the banking system in a drive to cut down on prohibitive interest rates.

"The rehabilitation of two banks -- Splitska and Rijecka -- will be completed this year," he said, adding that the biggest of the country's ailing banks, Privredna, would be included in the restructuring programme soon.

Deputy Prime Minister Borislav Skegro said a fiscal reform, started three years ago, would be completed in 1997 with the introduction of value added tax (VAT), designed to boost export-oriented industry and trade.

The government would continue to earmark more funds for economic development in next year's budget while cutting down current expenditures. But officials said this would not be done at the cost of exacerbating social problems.
Boosted by a seasonal workforce shrinkage in areas such as tourism without more jobs being opened, unemployment has hit a record high of 18.4 percent in September.
To compensate for layoffs caused by the restructuring of large state-owned companies, the government said it would up its drive to create new jobs and a better social system.

Other steps to help the growing number of disgruntled citizens suffering under a sharp drop in living standards would include a reform of the shaky pension system, although this may take years to complete, officials said.
"Our biggest problem are impatience and the unrealistic expectation that we can reach western European standards overnight," Skegro said.
"The war was not the only source of our problems and now that it is over, it will take more than a magic wand to improve things," he added.
